records.sourceFile: The Effect of Multi-Ingredient Protein versus Collagen Supplementation on Satellite Cell Properties in Males and Females.pdf

paper.citation: Wageh M, Fortino SA, Pontello R, Maklad A, McGlory C, Kumbhare D, et al. The Effect of Multi-Ingredient Protein versus Collagen Supplementation on Satellite Cell Properties in Males and Females. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2024;56(11):2125-2134.
paper.abstract: This randomized trial compared a multi-ingredient supplement with collagen during resistance training.
paper.tldr: The multi-ingredient group gained more type-II fiber area, but satellite-cell responses were mostly similar. This does not prove protein alone is responsible or required.
paper.methods: Twenty-six adults completed 10 weeks of linear resistance training while taking twice-daily whey, creatine, leucine, calcium, and vitamin-D supplement or collagen; vastus-lateralis biopsies assessed satellite cells, myonuclei, and fiber area.
paper.findings: The multi-ingredient group had greater type-II fiber cross-sectional-area gain. Satellite-cell content, myonuclear accretion, and most acute satellite-cell responses were similar between groups.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, the supplement included several active ingredients, many differences were not statistically robust, and biopsies do not establish sport performance or recovery benefit.
paper.practicalImplications: Prioritize adequate food and total protein intake, then assess whether any supplement fits a specific nutrition plan. Avoid attributing this result to a single ingredient.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that training remains the main anabolic stimulus and supplement response varies. Report gastrointestinal issues and avoid stacking products without a clear purpose.
paper.rtp: Do not use this study to prescribe a muscle-repair supplement after injury. Nutrition should support adequate intake alongside progressive rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: An association between bioavailable 25-hydroxyvitamin D and bone mineral density in a diverse cohort of collegiate athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Rockwell MS, Kostelnik SB, McMillan RP, Lancaster M, Larson-Meyer DE, Hulver MW. An Association between Bioavailable 25-Hydroxyvitamin D and Bone Mineral Density in a Diverse Cohort of Collegiate Athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2022;54(3):371-376.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared total and bioavailable vitamin-D measures with bone density in collegiate basketball and swimming athletes.
paper.tldr: Bioavailable vitamin D correlated with bone density in this small cohort, whereas total vitamin D did not. It is an association, not a supplementation trial.
paper.methods: Fifty-three Division-I basketball and swimming athletes underwent DXA, blood testing, and diet/lifestyle questionnaires; total and bioavailable 25-hydroxyvitamin D were compared with total bone mineral density.
paper.findings: Total and bioavailable vitamin-D classification disagreed for 53% of participants and 77% of Black participants. Bioavailable vitamin D correlated with total bone mineral density (r=0.618), while total vitamin D did not.
paper.limitations: The small two-sport, cross-sectional cohort cannot establish cause, fracture prevention, or supplementation need. Calculated bioavailability and cutoffs need clinical interpretation.
paper.practicalImplications: Evaluate bone health and vitamin-D status with qualified clinical and nutrition staff, especially where risk factors exist. Interpret results with diet, sun exposure, skin pigmentation, menstrual or endocrine status, and medical history.
paper.athleteDev: Avoid self-prescribing high-dose vitamin D from one result. Help athletes understand why testing and follow-up are individualized.
paper.rtp: Bone-health decisions during rehabilitation require diagnosis and medical oversight; this association does not supply a return-to-sport supplement protocol.

records.sourceFile: Inside the belly of a Beast - Individualizing nutrition for young professional male Rugby League players - A review.pdf

paper.citation: Kelly VG, Oliver LS, Bowtell J, Jenkins DG. Inside the Belly of a Beast: Individualizing Nutrition for Young, Professional Male Rugby League Players: A Review. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2020.
paper.abstract: This narrative review considers energy, macronutrient, recovery, and supplement strategies for young professional male rugby-league players.
paper.tldr: Rugby-league nutrition should be individualized around high energy demand, contact, and season phase. The suggested targets are practical starting ranges, not sport-specific certainty.
paper.methods: The review synthesized literature on rugby-league physiological demands, nutrition requirements, recovery, and potential ergogenic supplements across preparatory and competitive phases.
paper.findings: It proposes approximately 6-8 g/kg/day carbohydrate, 1.6-2.6 g/kg/day protein, and 0.7-2.2 g/kg/day fat, with phase-specific pre- and postexercise carbohydrate and protein strategies. It identifies insufficient rugby-league-specific energy-expenditure data.
paper.limitations: It is a narrative review with substantial extrapolation beyond rugby league; female athletes and individual seasonal energy needs are underrepresented.
paper.practicalImplications: Start with food-first, periodized intake matched to training, body-composition goal, and recovery demand. Monitor body mass, appetite, availability, gastrointestinal tolerance, and health.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to adjust intake as training and match demands change rather than follow one fixed daily menu.
paper.rtp: During injury, adjust energy and protein to changing activity and healing needs with a nutrition professional; do not automatically retain match-day targets.

records.sourceFile: UEFA expert group statement on nutrition in elite football - Current evidence to inform practical recommendations and guide future research.pdf

paper.citation: Collins J, Maughan RJ, Gleeson M, Bilsborough J, Jeukendrup A, Morton JP, et al. UEFA Expert Group Statement on Nutrition in Elite Football: Current Evidence to Inform Practical Recommendations and Guide Future Research. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;55:416-442.
paper.abstract: This UEFA expert statement provides a food-first, individualized nutrition framework for elite soccer.
paper.tldr: Periodize food, fluid, and carefully selected supplements around player demands, health, and practical constraints. A consensus statement is a framework, not a rigid prescription.
paper.methods: An international expert group synthesized current sports-nutrition evidence and its practical application to elite football training, match play, travel, recovery, body composition, and supplements.
paper.findings: The statement emphasizes matching food and fluid intake to training and match demands, protecting health and energy availability, and using only evidence-based supplements within a food-first strategy and antidoping-aware process.
paper.limitations: This is consensus rather than one controlled trial, and evidence quality differs by topic. Elite-soccer recommendations may require substantial adaptation for other populations and settings.
paper.practicalImplications: Build individualized, periodized plans with food access, travel, culture, body-composition goals, medical needs, and competition schedule in view. Use supplements only with a clear rationale and quality assurance.
paper.athleteDev: Make nutrition decisions understandable and practical: what to eat, drink, and prepare before, during, and after the actual demands of the week.
paper.rtp: Nutrition can support rehabilitation energy needs and recovery, but it cannot replace medical criteria, progressive loading, or return-to-play decision-making.

records.sourceFile: Blood, Sweat. and Tears - Implications for Hydration Testing in Combat Sports - Investigating Body Mass Loss and Biomarker Changes.pdf

paper.citation: Doherty CS, Fortington LV, Barley OR. Blood, Sweat, and Tears: Implications for Hydration Testing in Combat Sports—Investigating Body Mass Loss and Biomarker Changes. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2024.
paper.abstract: This repeated-trial study tested hydration biomarkers after passive dehydration in combat-sport athletes.
paper.tldr: Common hydration cutoffs misclassified many athletes after dehydration, and biomarker reliability varied. One test should not determine safety or eligibility.
paper.methods: Fifteen male and female combat athletes completed two sauna protocols 5-28 days apart targeting 4% body-mass loss; serum and urine osmolality, tear osmolarity, hematocrit, and urine-specific gravity were measured.
paper.findings: Average body-mass loss was 3.0%. Body-mass loss explained hematocrit change but not most other marker changes; post-dehydration hematocrit showed highest reliability, while urine-specific-gravity cutoff 1.020 misclassified 42%.
paper.limitations: The sample was small, passive sauna dehydration may not represent competition weight cutting, and the intended dehydration target was not reached. Cutoff performance depends on timing and cohort.
paper.practicalImplications: Use validated, context-specific hydration protocols and multiple clinical signals. Prioritize safe weight-management policy over a single biomarker result.
paper.athleteDev: Explain why an apparently normal urine measure does not prove safe hydration after a cut. Encourage early reporting of symptoms and honest weight-management planning.
paper.rtp: Hydration status should be managed medically and operationally, especially after rapid loss; no one biomarker establishes readiness to train or compete.

records.sourceFile: The Association of Vitamin D Status              in Lower Extremity Muscle Strains and Core Muscle Injuries at   the          National   Football League Combine.pdf

paper.citation: Rebolledo BJ, Bernard JA, Werner BC, Finlay AK, Nwachukwu BU, Dare DM, et al. The Association of Vitamin D Status in Lower Extremity Muscle Strains and Core Muscle Injuries at the National Football League Combine. Arthroscopy. 2018.
paper.abstract: This retrospective NFL Combine study examined vitamin-D status and prior muscle-injury history.
paper.tldr: Low vitamin D was common and linked with injury history in unadjusted analyses, but not independently after adjustment. It does not prove vitamin D caused strains.
paper.methods: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D and retrospective lower-extremity strain or core-injury histories were reviewed in 214 2015 NFL Combine athletes; regression models adjusted for recorded baseline factors.
paper.findings: Fifty-nine percent had inadequate vitamin D. Unadjusted inadequate status was associated with lower-extremity strain/core-injury and hamstring history, but multivariable low vitamin D was not independently associated with injury history.
paper.limitations: Retrospective history and a selected male combine cohort preclude temporality or causation. The study does not evaluate supplementation or future injury risk.
paper.practicalImplications: Use vitamin-D testing as one clinical data point when risk factors justify it. Correct deficiencies under medical and nutrition supervision rather than promising strain prevention.
paper.athleteDev: Avoid interpreting a result as proof of why an injury happened. Support consistent food, safe sun exposure, and follow-up when clinicians identify a need.
paper.rtp: Muscle return decisions need current symptoms, strength, function, and sport exposure; vitamin-D status alone cannot clear return.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Protein Supplementation During Early Rehabilitation on Muscle Volume and Function After Acute Muscle Strain Injuries - A Randomized Controlled Trial.pdf

paper.citation: Mertz KH, Sorensen HH, Lorentz C, Johansen E, Fredskild NU, Wulff MW, et al. Effects of Protein Supplementation During Early Rehabilitation on Muscle Volume and Function After Acute Muscle Strain Injuries: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2025.
paper.abstract: This double-blind trial tested whey protein during early rehabilitation after acute hamstring or calf strain injury.
paper.tldr: Twice-daily whey did not preserve muscle volume, improve strength, or shorten return after strain injury in recreational athletes. Adequate diet still matters, but this protocol was not a shortcut.
paper.methods: Fifty recreational athletes with acute hamstring or calf strains received twice-daily whey protein or isocaloric placebo during three months of early rehabilitation; MRI, strength, return time, and aponeurosis volume were followed to 12 months.
paper.findings: Injured-muscle volume decreased 9.4% during intervention and remained lower at 12 months. Protein did not change muscle volume, strength, return-to-sport time, or aponeurosis volume.
paper.limitations: The study involved recreational athletes and mixed injury sites. It tests one supplementation protocol, not adequacy of total dietary protein or other nutrition interventions in elite sport.
paper.practicalImplications: Meet overall energy and protein needs through a rehabilitation nutrition plan, but do not expect supplemental whey alone to preserve muscle or accelerate return.
paper.athleteDev: Set expectations that rehabilitation progress comes from appropriate loading, recovery, and adequate intake—not one product.
paper.rtp: Return depends on tissue status, strength, performance, and sport exposure. This trial does not support using whey response as a return marker.

records.sourceFile: The effects of creatine supplementation on cognitive performance - A randomized controlled study.pdf

paper.citation: Sandkühler JF, Kersting X, Faust A, Königs EK, Altman G, Ettinger U, et al. The Effects of Creatine Supplementation on Cognitive Performance—A Randomised Controlled Study. BMC Medicine. 2023;21:440.
paper.abstract: This double-blind crossover trial evaluated six-week creatine supplementation and cognitive performance.
paper.tldr: Creatine showed at most a small cognitive benefit in non-athlete participants and caused more reported side effects. It is not evidence for a sport-cognition or concussion protocol.
paper.methods: One hundred twenty-three vegetarians and omnivores completed randomized double-blind six-week periods of 5 g/day creatine and placebo, with Raven matrices, backward digit span, and exploratory cognitive tasks.
paper.findings: Bayesian analysis supported a small benefit; backward digit span bordered significance, Raven matrices and exploratory tests did not. Vegetarians did not benefit more, and side effects were more frequent with creatine.
paper.limitations: Participants were not an athlete-performance sample, effects were small and task-specific, and the study does not establish benefit for sport decisions or head injury.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not add creatine for cognitive performance solely from this result. When creatine is considered for another objective, review individual tolerance, goals, and product quality.
paper.athleteDev: Separate potential training benefits from unproven promises about focus or brain protection. Report side effects and avoid unplanned supplement stacking.
paper.rtp: Creatine is not a concussion treatment or readiness marker. Follow established medical and staged return protocols.

records.sourceFile: Does Caffeine Supplementation Affect Sleep in Athletes - A Systematic Review of Nine Randomized Controlled trials.pdf

paper.citation: Bodur M, Barkell J, Li X, Sajadi Hezaveh Z. Does Caffeine Supplementation Affect Sleep in Athletes? A Systematic Review of Nine Randomized Controlled Trials. Clinical Nutrition ESPEN. 2024.
paper.abstract: This systematic review examined randomized athlete trials of caffeine supplementation and sleep.
paper.tldr: Caffeine can impair sleep, with response shaped by dose, timing, and individual sensitivity. Performance planning should protect recovery rather than assume standard use is harmless.
paper.methods: The authors systematically reviewed nine randomized controlled trials assessing caffeine supplementation and athlete sleep outcomes.
paper.findings: Across heterogeneous trials, caffeine was associated with impaired sleep measures, and the review highlights dose, timing, and individual sensitivity as practical considerations.
paper.limitations: Only nine heterogeneous trials were available and the source is an accepted pre-proof. Protocols, athlete samples, sleep measures, and study quality do not establish a universally safe dose or timing.
paper.practicalImplications: Trial caffeine in training and schedule it around both performance and upcoming sleep opportunity. Use the lowest effective dose and account for individual sensitivity.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to notice delayed sleep onset, reduced sleep quality, and next-day recovery effects rather than focusing only on the immediate lift from caffeine.
paper.rtp: Protect sleep during rehabilitation and return progression; stimulant use should not mask fatigue or substitute for recovery.

records.sourceFile: Nutritional Supplement and Dietary Interventions as a Prophylaxis or Treatment of Sub-Concussive Repetitive Head Impact and Mild Traumatic Brain Injury - A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Feinberg C, Dickerson Mayes K, Jarvis RC III, Carr C, Mannix R. Nutritional Supplement and Dietary Interventions as a Prophylaxis or Treatment of Sub-Concussive Repetitive Head Impact and Mild Traumatic Brain Injury: A Systematic Review. Journal of Neurotrauma. 2023.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated nutrition and dietary interventions for repetitive head impact and mild traumatic brain injury.
paper.tldr: Some studies reported benefit, especially for omega-3 approaches, but the evidence is too heterogeneous and biased to make a concussion supplement protocol.
paper.methods: PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched without a specified time period. Fifteen studies from 12 populations, totaling 1,139 participants, met eligibility criteria.
paper.findings: Eleven studies reported benefit across eight interventions. Omega-3 fatty acids, melatonin, and Pinus radiata had multiple studies; the authors identify omega-3 as the strongest prevention evidence while calling for larger multicenter studies.
paper.limitations: Interventions, timing, populations, and outcomes varied. Over half of studies had some bias concern and all industry-sponsored studies reported supportive findings, preventing firm efficacy conclusions.
paper.practicalImplications: Maintain a food-first approach and do not market supplements as head-injury prevention or treatment. Any use should be medically supervised and secondary to established safety and clinical care.
paper.athleteDev: Clarify that no supplement makes repetitive head impacts safe or replaces reporting symptoms and following medical guidance.
paper.rtp: Nutrition may support general recovery but cannot alter concussion clearance requirements or replace staged return-to-learn and return-to-sport care.

records.sourceFile: Can I have my coffee and drink it - A systematic review and meta-analysis to determine whether habitual caffeine consumption affects the ergogenic effect of caffeine.pdf

paper.citation: Carvalho A, Marticorena FM, Grecco BH, Barreto G, Saunders B. Can I Have My Coffee and Drink It? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis to Determine Whether Habitual Caffeine Consumption Affects the Ergogenic Effect of Caffeine. Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis tested whether habitual caffeine intake changes the acute ergogenic response to caffeine.
paper.tldr: Habitual caffeine use did not appear to erase acute performance benefit in pooled studies. Individual sleep, side effects, dose, and timing still determine whether caffeine is useful.
paper.methods: Three databases were searched; 60 caffeine studies reporting habitual intake entered three-level meta-analyses and meta-regressions across exercise types, sex, training status, dose, and withdrawal periods.
paper.findings: Caffeine improved performance versus placebo overall (SMD 0.25), with no habitual-intake moderation. Benefits appeared below 3 and at 3-6 mg/kg but not above 6 mg/kg in subgroup analysis.
paper.limitations: Habitual intake and body mass commonly used group means, few studies directly tested habituation, caffeine estimates were imprecise, and no included study was low risk of bias.
paper.practicalImplications: Individualize caffeine trialing around a performance target and sleep schedule. Avoid assuming high doses, habitual use, or abstinence guarantees a better response.
paper.athleteDev: Have athletes track dose, timing, perceived benefit, anxiety, gastrointestinal response, and sleep so decisions reflect their response rather than group averages.
paper.rtp: Caffeine should not be used to conceal fatigue during return progression. Protect sleep and use clinical and performance criteria to guide load.
